previousReview.title: Extent of prior colon assessment

cues.phrase: Adherent opaque material remained over broad areas of the ascending and transverse mucosa after washing.
cues.why: This clearly unsuccessful cleaning is paired with the only option offering an 'enhanced bowel-preparation plan'; the wording lets a lay reader match problem to repair.

cues.phrase: with the previous preparation plan
cues.why: The sigmoidoscopy distractor unnecessarily advertises reuse of the visibly inadequate preparation, making it wrong on two independent grounds.

fairness: Repeat adequately prepared colonoscopy is a defensible key after complicated diverticulitis and a prior examination with poorly visualized proximal mucosa. Reaching the cecum does not establish adequate mucosal assessment.
Importance: high; distinguishing procedural extent from adequacy is useful. Realism: credible recovered clinic patient, with a suitable interval described rather than active inflammation.
Too easy: the report-to-summary discrepancy is worthwhile, but the broad unwashed areas and self-discrediting distractor leave a single obvious repair.
suggestions: Keep the actual segment-level preparation observations; remove the 'previous preparation plan' qualifier from the distractor.
Compare plausible complete-colon assessment or timing strategies with equivalent preparation specificity, rather than a distal-only test and reliance on an obviously contradicted summary.
Make a genuine adequacy/timing boundary determine the plan; do not invent a preparation score or cutoff.

decisionNodes.stem: Which post-recovery examination plan is best for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Repeat colonoscopy with an enhanced bowel-preparation plan
answerChoices.rationale: Reaching the cecum does not establish an adequate mucosal examination. The preparation narrative limits the prior assessment, and his recovered complicated episode supports colonoscopy for an alternative lesion.

answerChoices.label: Perform flexible sigmoidoscopy with the previous preparation plan
answerChoices.rationale: This re-examines the distal region rather than addressing the quality limitation in the earlier colon examination.

answerChoices.label: Use the prior colonoscopy and arrange symptom-led follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The reassuring summary and cecal landmarks do not overcome the recorded mucosal obscuration.

decisionNodes.explanation: The prior scope reached the cecum, but preparation prevented adequate inspection of substantial mucosa. Those are different dimensions of examination quality. After this recovered complicated diverticulitis episode, a repeat adequately prepared colonoscopy is the selected luminal evaluation. The prior stop was not a fixed anatomical barrier; no guarantee of completion or universal timing interval is taught.

items.label: Distal observations

answerChoices.rationale: The urinary discomfort can accompany adjacent colonic inflammation. The focal abdominal findings and uncertain first episode call for assessment of bowel inflammation and complications, beyond a stone-focused examination.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis
answerChoices.rationale: The first episode has overlapping urinary and colonic features. Abdominopelvic CT can establish the source and assess for a collection or other complication.

answerChoices.label: Colonoscopy with inspection of the entire colon
answerChoices.rationale: Colonoscopy may have a later role in luminal assessment. It does not supply the initial cross-sectional assessment of a possible acute extraluminal inflammatory complication.

historicalClaims.statement: After a first recovered complicated diverticulitis episode with abscess and no recent adequate examination, colonoscopy can be selected to exclude an alternative lesion.
historicalClaims.applicablePopulation: Stable patients recovered from a first complicated left-sided diverticulitis episode without recent adequate colonoscopy.

historicalClaims.statement: After recovery, elective sigmoid-resection discussion should use complications, ongoing burden, operative risk, and patient preferences rather than a simple episode count.
historicalClaims.limitation: A shared discussion is not a mandatory operation.
historicalClaims.applicablePopulation: Stable recovered diverticulitis patients considering elective surgery.

historicalClaims.statement: CT should confirm a first suspected presentation of acute diverticulitis and assess for complications when no prior imaging-confirmed diagnosis exists.
historicalClaims.limitation: This does not require CT for every recurrent classic episode after an established diagnosis and does not delay emergency treatment in an unstable patient.
historicalClaims.applicablePopulation: Stable adults with a first suspected mild presentation of acute diverticulitis and no prior imaging-confirmed episode.

historicalClaims.statement: Routine antibiotics can be omitted in selected immunocompetent, nonfrail outpatients with mild CT-confirmed uncomplicated diverticulitis, no systemic inflammation or high-risk imaging feature, oral-intake tolerance, and reliable follow-up.
historicalClaims.limitation: This selection does not apply to complicated disease, immunocompromise, frailty, systemic inflammation, inability to tolerate intake, or unreliable follow-up.
historicalClaims.applicablePopulation: Carefully selected stable outpatients with mild CT-confirmed uncomplicated diverticulitis.

rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Choose colectomy for a gross sigmoid perforation with diffuse fecal contamination instead of a lavage-based plan.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Distinguish a gross fecal leak from contained gas or selected purulent peritonitis.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Generalizing a selected nonresection strategy to any generalized diverticular contamination.
rankedConcepts.consequence: A lavage-based plan can leave the continuing fecal source uncontrolled.

rankedConcepts.title: Reconstruction after emergency diverticular resection
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Post-resuscitation host and bowel selection govern restoration of continuity and long-term stoma burden.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Select reconstruction after emergency sigmoid resection using patient physiology, host risk and bowel condition.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Assess current perfusion, tension and host physiology after source control instead of carrying the original contamination label forward as the whole decision.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Treating the original fecal contamination as an automatic requirement for an end colostomy.
rankedConcepts.consequence: An automatic end-colostomy policy can forgo a supported restoration strategy in a suitable patient.
rankedConcepts.revisionCoverage: Retained draft coverage; exact review/assembly status in proposals.

rankedConcepts.title: CTA during ongoing significant hematochezia
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Selecting the correct diagnostic pathway during ongoing significant hemorrhage can change immediate treatment.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Select CTA to localize ongoing hemodynamically significant suspected colonic bleeding when preparation is unsuitable.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Distinguish persistent hemodynamically important blood loss from a stopped bleed after initial resuscitation, while accounting for upper-source evaluation.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Applying the stable-bleeding colonoscopy pathway to continuing hemodynamic blood loss.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Repeated preparation attempts can postpone localization during continued blood loss.
rankedConcepts.revisionCoverage: Retained draft coverage; exact review/assembly status in proposals.

rankedConcepts.title: Angiographic treatment selection for ongoing colonic bleeding
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: A positive acquisition and the continuing course determine whether a radiologic hemostatic opportunity should be used.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Select angiographic assessment with possible embolization for a localized ongoing significant colonic bleed unsuitable for immediate prepared colonoscopy.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Distinguish newly accumulating intraluminal contrast from pre-existing dense stool or a fixed incidental finding.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Returning to the familiar endoscopic pathway after CTA has localized continuing active blood loss.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Delaying a suitable hemostatic route can permit continuing blood loss.
rankedConcepts.revisionCoverage: Retained draft coverage; exact review/assembly status in proposals.

rankedConcepts.title: Prepared nonemergent colonoscopy after stabilization
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: The stopped-versus-ongoing bleed distinction prevents a universal emergency-imaging or emergency-endoscopy rule.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Select nonemergent prepared colonoscopy when a hospitalized lower-GI bleed has stopped and the patient is stable.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Recognize sustained cessation of bleeding and hemodynamic stability from serial observations.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Applying the severe ongoing-bleeding CTA pathway to every hospitalized bleed.
rankedConcepts.consequence: An indiscriminate CTA pathway can add a low-yield study while leaving the luminal investigation outstanding.
rankedConcepts.revisionCoverage: Retained draft coverage; exact review/assembly status in proposals.

rankedConcepts.title: Treatment of a nonbleeding diverticular vessel
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Recognizing a treatable stigma after active flow stops changes endoscopic care.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Recognize a high-risk diverticular hemorrhage finding and select definitive local endoscopic treatment despite cessation of active flow.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Recognize the persistent vessel as a bleeding stigma rather than an incidental diverticulum.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Equating the absence of active flow with the absence of a treatable high-risk lesion.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Stopping at visual cessation or transient control leaves a high-risk site untreated.
rankedConcepts.revisionCoverage: Retained draft coverage; exact review/assembly status in proposals.

rankedConcepts.title: Localized resection after failed bleeding control
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Operative extent after failed hemostasis must follow direct source evidence, not incidental diverticula.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Use concordant anatomic localization to select the bleeding segment for surgical rescue after failed endoscopic and radiologic therapy.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Separate direct source localization from incidental disease distribution and distinguish treatment failure from uncertainty about the source.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Treating severe recurrent bleeding as if its anatomic origin were still unknown.
rankedConcepts.consequence: The wrong segment can leave the culprit behind, while unnecessary extensive resection increases operative burden.
rankedConcepts.revisionCoverage: Retained draft coverage; exact review/assembly status in proposals.

rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Anchoring on dysuria and urinary leukocytes.
rankedConcepts.consequence: A stone-focused pathway can leave an inflammatory complication insufficiently characterized.

rankedConcepts.title: Selected supportive care for uncomplicated diverticulitis

rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Use outpatient supportive care without routine antibiotics for a carefully selected mild uncomplicated case.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Combine the absence of a CT complication with the actual improving course and ability to maintain intake.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Treating every CT-confirmed inflammatory episode with an antibiotic.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Routine treatment adds avoidable antibiotic exposure to a patient with a relevant prior complication.

rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Use immune status and observed disease severity to select antibiotic treatment for uncomplicated diverticulitis.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Distinguish uncomplicated imaging from membership in the immunocompetent antibiotic-omission population.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Extending the selected antibiotic-omission evidence to every radiologically uncomplicated episode.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Applying omission data to an excluded host can undertreat a patient at higher complication concern.

rankedConcepts.title: Colonoscopy after recovered complicated diverticulitis

rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Separate collection resolution from assessment of the colonic lumen, and identify the actual extent of the earlier endoscopy.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Treating radiologic resolution of the inflammatory complication as the only required follow-up endpoint.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Repeating the extraluminal study can leave a relevant mucosal lesion unassessed.

rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Distinguish resolved acute infection from an atypical persistent bowel problem.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Extending radiologic surveillance because the acute collection resolved.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Reassurance from prior screening can delay evaluation of a new lesion or symptomatic narrowing.

rankedConcepts.title: Elective sigmoid treatment selection after recovery
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Burden, operative risk and informed priorities change an actual treatment plan.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Select a concrete elective sigmoid treatment plan using ongoing burden, operative risk and informed patient priorities.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Identify discrete recovered recurrences with substantial functional burden rather than ongoing uncontrolled infection.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Reading individualized guidance as a reason to defer every operation after recovery.
rankedConcepts.consequence: A fixed policy of waiting leaves the patient's recurrent burden untreated despite an appropriate elective option.

rankedConcepts.title: Resection for symptomatic diverticular fistula
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Persistent structural communication requires a different decision from treating each infection.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Select elective sigmoid resection for a persistent symptomatic colovesical communication after acute infection control.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Distinguish treated infection from persistence of its documented structural source.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Continuing an effective short-term infection treatment as the definitive plan.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Repeated infection treatment leaves the symptomatic communication untreated.
rankedConcepts.revisionCoverage: Gap remains after one repair; parked attempts do not count as coverage.

rankedConcepts.title: Resection for a symptomatic sigmoid stricture
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Mechanical obstruction after recovery requires distinction from a new inflammatory episode.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Select resection for persistent obstructive symptoms from a fixed sigmoid narrowing after acute inflammation resolves.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Identify a fixed mechanical consequence after acute inflammation has subsided.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Transferring a treatment used for selected other benign strictures to this setting.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Treating an assumed recurrent flare or an incompletely characterized stricture can postpone effective treatment of obstruction.
rankedConcepts.revisionCoverage: Retained draft coverage; exact review/assembly status in proposals.

rankedConcepts.title: Healthy boundaries for elective sigmoid resection
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Proximal disease boundaries and a rectal distal target are practical operative planning decisions.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Choose resection boundaries that remove diseased sigmoid and reach healthy rectum while preserving uninvolved proximal colon.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Distinguish diverticula from inflamed or fibrotic disease and identify the rectal distal target.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Minimizing resection to the visibly thickest area without considering the distal sigmoid remnant.
rankedConcepts.consequence: A retained sigmoid anastomotic target can leave an unfavorable disease boundary, while extension removes uninvolved colon.
rankedConcepts.revisionCoverage: Retained draft coverage; exact review/assembly status in proposals.

rankedConcepts.title: Aspirin indication after controlled diverticular bleeding
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Medication indication changes the acceptable bleeding-versus-cardiovascular tradeoff.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Preserve aspirin for established cardiovascular disease after controlled lower-GI bleeding while avoiding nonaspirin NSAID exposure.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Distinguish established cardiovascular secondary prevention from symptom treatment with a nonaspirin NSAID.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Removing all potentially bleeding-associated medicines without assessing the reason each is prescribed.
rankedConcepts.consequence: A blanket bleeding-risk response can remove cardiovascular protection or retain avoidable recurrent-bleeding exposure.
rankedConcepts.revisionCoverage: Retained draft coverage; exact review/assembly status in proposals.

rankedConcepts.title: Primary-prevention aspirin after diverticular bleeding
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Risk factors must be distinguished from an established secondary-prevention indication.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of general-surgery decision value. No exam frequency or percentage is asserted.
rankedConcepts.residentDecision: Discontinue primary-prevention aspirin after diverticular hemorrhage when no established cardiovascular indication is present.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidenceToInterpret: Distinguish cardiovascular risk factors from established atherosclerotic disease requiring secondary prevention.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Treating several cardiovascular risk factors as equivalent to established cardiovascular disease.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Misclassification can perpetuate a bleeding-associated medicine without the intended secondary-prevention benefit.

rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Applying the familiar focal-vessel strategy to a broad mucosal vascular lesion.

reviewRows.title: Initial imaging for overlapping colonic and urinary symptoms
fairness: Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT is the best offered investigation: interpret focal inflammatory abdominal findings despite urinary symptoms, then select broad cross-sectional evaluation rather than a stone-focused study or acute colonoscopy. This is high-yield moderate application.
Absence of hematuria does not exclude a stone; the explanation appropriately rests on the overall presentation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The retrospective clinic frame is understandable. The subsequent CT-result node follows coherently, and this explanation does not reveal its antibiotic decision.

Review scope for the entire array: all 25 candidates, comprising 4 rewrites and 21 new nodes. Only after/candidate visible text and preceding visible explanations informed judgments, not author gates or difficulty claims. Fourteen retire-and-replace historical records, one retained historical drop hold and three unkeyed boundaries were noted but not scored; there are no kept-unchanged candidates. No network or fresh source verification was performed. PASS is editorial only; all clinical drafts remain needs_clinician_review. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative, not measured exam frequencies.

reviewRows.title: Selective antibiotic omission with previous C. difficile
clarityIssues: The task requests an initial outpatient plan while offering inpatient treatment; it also says initial after describing a subsequent reassessment. Anchor the decision at that reassessment.

cues.phrase: Which initial outpatient plan best fits {patientName}'s CT findings and subsequent assessment?
cues.why: The word outpatient eliminates 'Use inpatient intravenous antibiotics with serial reassessment' without interpreting clinical data.

fairness: Supportive care with reassessment is the best offered plan: interpret an improving uncomplicated course and then weigh antibiotic benefit against recurrent antibiotic-associated harm. Oral antibiotics remain a recognizable competitor.
The preceding imaging explanation does not disclose antibiotic omission. The update supplies enough CT and clinical information to stand alone with the shared presentation.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The high-yield two-step decision is moderate, but one distractor is nonfunctional because of task wording.
suggestions: Ask which care plan fits the reassessment without preselecting disposition.
Keep trajectory, immune status, intake and prior C. difficile history. Compare credible plans at the same decision stage and recheck the admission distractor after removing the cue.

reviewRows.title: Colonic examination after recovery from a diverticular abscess

cues.phrase: His records contained no colorectal screening examination.
cues.why: Names a missing examination immediately supplied by the colonoscopy option; this becomes completion of an announced omission.

cues.phrase: His only prior endoscopy report described the esophagus, stomach and duodenum.
cues.why: The elementary upper-versus-lower mismatch rehearses why the previous examination cannot satisfy this task.

cues.phrase: Repeat contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis
cues.why: CT resolution has already been reported, with no residual problem to reassess. This is a completed-work foil.

fairness: Complete colonoscopy after recovery is the best offered answer in this unscreened patient with a complicated episode. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The later elective-treatment decision follows coherently and is not disclosed by this explanation. This node is self-contained.
The concept is high yield, but recognizing upper endoscopy and recalling a follow-up rule do not constitute two consequential resident-level steps.
suggestions: Use a clinically meaningful adequacy or timing problem in an actual prior colonic evaluation, supported by observations that change the next action.
Do not cross the separately held recent-adequate-colonoscopy boundary without clinician resolution. If no difficult fair variant is supportable, request an explicit basic-item role.
Replace the already successful CT assessment with a credible diagnostic alternative at the same recovery stage.

reviewRows.title: Elective sigmoid resection after recurrent burdensome disease

cues.phrase: he preferred resection to further recurrences
cues.why: Directly names the treatment keyed as 'Schedule an elective sigmoid colectomy'; the preference can be matched without clinical weighing.

cues.phrase: Start oral mesalamine maintenance therapy
cues.why: A weak clinical competitor for recurrent diverticular disease; it supplies little discrimination. This is distractor implausibility rather than a lexical shortcut by itself.

fairness: Elective resection is reasonable given burden, recovery, risk assessment and informed preference. The concern is answer disclosure, not a confident clinical error.
The prior colonoscopy task coherently leads to the negative examination reported here. The update stands alone with the shared presentation.
Elective decision-making is high yield, but the stem has already completed the weighing and selected the procedure.
suggestions: Retain meaningful informed preferences but express priorities without naming the operation.
Introduce a supported competing consideration that actually changes management, such as interpretation of recurrent inflammatory versus persistent noninflammatory symptoms.
Do not merely delete preference and leave equally reasonable elective policies.

reviewRows.title: Initial investigation of suspected bowel-bladder communication
fairness: Interpret recurrent infections and pneumaturia without instrumentation as possible bowel-bladder communication, then choose cross-sectional evaluation of cause and extent. Cystoscopy is a credible narrower alternative; CT best addresses the combined abdominal and urinary findings.
Absence of catheterization is decision-critical context rather than improper distractor deletion. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The explanation supports the diagnostic inference without prescribing the later operation. Subsequent CT and treatment follow-up are coherent.
This is high-yield moderate application; the classic symptom pattern does not justify a hard rating.

reviewRows.title: Definitive treatment of persistent sigmoid-to-bladder communication

cues.phrase: Plan bladder repair with the sigmoid left in place
cues.why: The appended omission announces that the plan leaves the named diseased source untreated; it reads as a critique rather than a neutral treatment label.

cues.phrase: Use repeated culture-directed urinary antibiotic courses
cues.why: Repeats the strategy already described as failing to end recurrent infections, leaving only one apparently definitive plan.

fairness: Resection of the involved sigmoid is the best offered definitive treatment after infection control in this fit symptomatic patient. The explanation appropriately separates precise bladder technique.
The update supplies the communication and tumor assessment, so the later node is coherent and independently usable. Earlier feedback already directs attention to adjacent bowel and bladder.

A supplied structural diagnosis followed by its standard operation against conspicuously incomplete alternatives is easy high-yield recall, not two consequential steps. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Introduce a supported patient-specific timing or operative-strategy tradeoff if two-step difficulty is required.
Use neutral complete treatment plans and avoid appending an explicit omission to mark the wrong answer.
Do not invent a ranking of bladder techniques merely to increase difficulty.

reviewRows.title: Diagnostic examination despite a prior adequate colonoscopy
clarityIssues: The previous colonoscopy is only dated 'before this illness'. If recency matters to the intended challenge, the reader cannot assess it.
The 'next routine surveillance visit' does not identify a relevant surveillance program or justify delaying evaluation of current symptoms.

cues.phrase: Perform colonoscopy to assess the persistent colonic change
cues.why: Only the key states a rationale matching the persistent symptoms. The CT option defers to routine surveillance and stool DNA offers screening instead of an equally plausible diagnostic plan.

fairness: New altered stool caliber, weight loss and focal thickening justify diagnostic evaluation despite an earlier negative examination. Colonoscopy is the best offered answer; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
There is a meaningful two-step high-yield objective: reinterpret new alarm findings despite prior reassurance, then choose a diagnostic examination. Weak alternatives lower discrimination.
The subsequent narrowing/obstruction node follows logically. This explanation does not disclose its treatment.
suggestions: State relevant chronology without inventing a mandatory interval.
Use equally neutral diagnostic-plan labels; remove the key's rationale clause and unexplained routine-surveillance delay.
Replace the screening-only foil with a credible diagnostic competitor whose limitation must be inferred from the case.

reviewRows.title: Treatment of persistent fixed sigmoid obstruction
fairness: Distinguish fixed mechanical obstruction from recurrent inflammation using narrowing, proximal dilation and absent surrounding inflammatory findings, then choose resection rather than another antibiotic course or dilation. Dilation is a credible competing error.

Resection is the best offered plan. These findings do not prove a benign cause or exclude malignancy, but that uncertainty does not rescue the dilation alternative. The explanation preserves the need to evaluate the underlying cause and should not be read as establishing benign pathology.
The prior investigation leads coherently to this colonoscopy result. The update independently supplies narrowing and current obstructive physiology.
High-yield moderate surgical application; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

reviewRows.title: Source control for a large localized diverticular abscess
fairness: Interpret a sizable localized collection with preserved physiology, then choose drainage plus antibiotics rather than antibiotics without drainage or immediate resection. Size, containment and clinical state jointly determine the action.
A documented safe percutaneous route is necessary to distinguish source-control approaches; it does not itself establish the indication for drainage. Retain this meaningful feasibility fact.
The 6-cm measurement is a case observation, not a newly asserted cutoff. No borderline threshold claim or confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.
Later worsening is a coherent new event rather than a contradiction of the initial plan. This is high-yield moderate reasoning, not hard.

reviewRows.title: Escalation when the drain misses the worsening source

cues.phrase: Proceed to operative control of the undrained source
cues.why: The option supplies the interpretation 'undrained source' that the resident should derive. Only this option explicitly addresses the new collection.

cues.phrase: antibiotics active against the cultured organisms
cues.why: Together with a collapsed drained cavity and a separate inaccessible collection, this pre-disqualifies broadening antibiotics. The datum is useful, but the current options largely test serial elimination.

fairness: Worsening illness and an enlarging inaccessible collection support operative source control. Enlarging a catheter in a different collapsed cavity does not address the anatomy.
The high-yield objective has two consequential steps: recognize the drain-target mismatch and select escalation. Wording and option design unnecessarily reveal the inference.

The second node coherently follows initial drainage and restates the anatomy sufficiently to stand alone. The first explanation teaches source control but does not prescribe management of the new inaccessible collection.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Label the operative plan neutrally without 'undrained source'.
Retain anatomy and safe-access facts. Improve the competing plans so one requires genuine interpretation rather than contradicting an explicit statement.
Do not remove access information merely to make operative versus percutaneous management ambiguous.

reviewRows.title: Source control for feculent diverticular perforation
clarityIssues: 'The founder reviews the sequential operative records with him' adds no decision information, although the retrospective clinic frame is understandable.
fairness: Resection is the best offered procedure for the disrupted diseased sigmoid with diffuse fecal contamination. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

This is direct recognition of gross perforation followed by a standard operation. Urgency findings should remain, but lavage and simple closure are weak competitors for residents in this exact presentation.
The reconstruction node follows coherently. This explanation partly scaffolds it by naming physiology and bowel condition as the next decision dimensions.
This is a high-yield safety decision, not a hard two-step resident item.
suggestions: Request an explicitly accepted foundational/safety role or change the scored objective to a genuinely competing source-control decision supported by the findings.
Preserve fecal contamination and full-thickness perforation; never hide urgency to manufacture difficulty.
Remove decorative framing and avoid rehearsing the next scored discriminator.

reviewRows.title: Reconstruction after sigmoid resection in a selected stable patient
clarityIssues: Standalone context is incomplete: the presentation says emergency abdominal surgery and the update says 'After source resection'; the feculent diverticular perforation appears only in the prior node.
The learner explanation ends with an editorial review instruction instead of explaining the closest competing operation.

cues.phrase: Reconstruction is considered separately after resection and assessment of physiology and bowel condition.
cues.why: The preceding explanation rehearses the dimensions immediately tested. This is sequence scaffolding rather than a standalone answer leak, but lowers independent difficulty.

fairness: Primary anastomosis with diversion is a defensible preferred offered reconstruction in these favorable conditions. Hartmann is not intrinsically incorrect in every such patient; explain the conditional preference rather than an absolute.
Host risk, physiology and bowel suitability create a meaningful high-yield two-step decision. The favorable checklist and weak staged-reconstruction competitor keep it moderate.
The paired sequence is coherent, but independent-node contamination context is missing. No confident clinical inaccuracy is asserted in this offline review.
suggestions: Restate the emergency diverticular perforation and contamination context briefly in this node.
Explain the conditional preference over Hartmann and obtain clinician confirmation of the exact ranking.
Move review-status instructions out of learner feedback and reduce preceding answer-specific scaffolding within the authorized revision lane.

reviewRows.title: Antibiotic treatment and disposition in a transplant recipient
clarityIssues: Antibiotic eligibility is conflated with route and admission. The task does not establish a pathway uniquely resolving outpatient versus inpatient treatment.
Substantial chronic lung disease is introduced only in the next node, although baseline comorbidity could matter to this earlier disposition.

cues.phrase: after outpatient treatment of her first CT-confirmed sigmoid inflammatory episode
cues.why: The presentation reveals the historical disposition before asking the resident to choose outpatient versus inpatient care.

cues.phrase: she ate without vomiting and pain was controlled with oral medication
cues.why: Together with an arranged early reassessment, this previews oral/outpatient care without settling all host-risk concerns sufficiently to make admission wrong.

fairness: Antibiotics are well motivated by tacrolimus/mycophenolate use. Inpatient intravenous antibiotics and observation nevertheless remain defensible for an immunosuppressed transplant recipient; normal vital signs, oral tolerance and preserved renal function alone do not establish that the competing disposition is incorrect.

The explanation calls outpatient oral treatment the proposed plan rather than resolving that competing choice. This review does not claim outpatient care is prohibited; the scoring failure is the absence of one securely distinguishable best answer.
The next node's pulmonary comorbidity requires a coherent shared history; unseen later information cannot fairly score this node.
This is a high-yield two-step issue, but ambiguity is not legitimate hard difficulty. FAIL concerns the current scored version, not the topic.
suggestions: Rebuild around one decision: establish common disposition and compare antibiotic strategies, or make disposition the objective with clinician-supported information that actually resolves it.
Remove the retrospective outpatient answer disclosure.
Make chronic comorbidity consistent across the case and have Melissa confirm the exact transplant-management boundary. Do not invent an admission threshold.

reviewRows.title: Elective management after recovery in a high-risk transplant recipient
clarityIssues: Chronic lung disease first appears after an acute disposition decision where relevant baseline comorbidity should have been available.

cues.phrase: she preferred to continue nonsurgical care while symptoms remained absent
cues.why: Essentially states the keyed nonoperative plan; the resident need not weigh treatment choices.

cues.phrase: Pulmonary assessment documented substantial operative risk from chronic lung disease.
cues.why: Supplies the risk interpretation rather than observations, reinforcing the already stated nonsurgical answer.

cues.phrase: Continue nonoperative follow-up with a recurrence response plan
cues.why: The key alone includes a reassuring contingency plan, beside surgery and an unsupported maintenance-drug strategy.

fairness: Observation is reasonable after recovery given supplied risk and informed preference. Acute antibiotic eligibility does not itself mandate elective colectomy; this is a valuable high-yield distinction.
The later timeline is coherent and the update stands alone with the presentation, but it dictates the answer instead of requiring two consequential steps.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

reviewRows.title: Localization during continuing significant lower-GI hemorrhage
fairness: Interpret repeated hypotension during further large-volume bleeding despite replacement as ongoing significant hemorrhage, then select CTA instead of a delayed prepared examination or less precise scintigraphic localization.

Preserve serial stability and absence of further blood loss.

This important high-yield rule remains direct recognition followed by a standard treatment association. No competing morphology, failed therapy or other consequential constraint creates a second applied step.

Selective angiography with possible embolization is the best offered plan. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The node independently supplies prior treatment, recurrence, localization and current physiology. Subsequent failure of endoscopic and radiologic interventions is coherent.
High-yield moderate application. This overlaps the positive-CTA node elsewhere in the packet; that is content redundancy rather than a standalone scoring defect.

cues.phrase: CTA, endoscopy and angiography all localized active bleeding to the ascending segment.

cues.phrase: many sigmoid diverticula but no left-colon bleeding stigma

cues.phrase: CTA supplies a current anatomic target.

fairness: Right colectomy is the best offered extent after failed nonsurgical treatment with credible ascending-colon localization. Incidental sigmoid diverticula do not justify sigmoid resection.

suggestions: Provide interpretable raw localization records and a meaningful reliability distinction that changes operative extent.

reviewRows.title: Definitive reconstruction in a physiologically high-risk patient
fairness: Integrate vasopressor dependence, steroid exposure, severe lung disease and edematous bowel, then distinguish avoiding an anastomosis from merely diverting one. Hartmann is the best offered definitive reconstruction.

The standalone record supplies disease, operative stage and host risk. High-yield moderate reasoning; no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

reviewRows.title: Proximal and distal boundaries for elective sigmoid resection

cues.phrase: Remove the diseased sigmoid and join descending colon to rectum

This standalone case has an internal chronology defect rather than dependence on an earlier node.
suggestions: Repair convergence using a clinically credible balanced option design and re-attack with clinical findings hidden.

reviewRows.title: Distinguishing secondary-prevention aspirin from nonaspirin NSAIDs
fairness: Infer secondary prevention from prior myocardial infarction, then weigh cardiovascular benefit separately from avoidable naproxen exposure after hemorrhage. Continue aspirin and discontinue naproxen is the best offered discharge plan.

fairness: Distinguish risk factors and family history from established vascular disease, then reassess preventive aspirin after significant hemorrhage. Discontinuation is the best offered plan; clopidogrel substitution does not create a secondary-prevention indication.

The standalone record supplies indications and resolved hemorrhage. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; feedback does not impose an unsupported universal rule.
High-yield low-moderate application rather than hard reasoning; indication classification followed by a benefit/harm decision provides two consequential steps.

reviewRows.title: Endoscopic treatment of superficial cecal vascular lesions

cues.phrase: There was no focal exposed vessel within a diverticulum.

The standalone story is coherent. No actual exhibit is supplied, but no image is promised and the observations are readable.
The concept is high yield. No confident clinical inaccuracy is asserted; concerns are difficulty, tailored exclusion and insufficient explanation of the closest modality.
suggestions: Remove the tailored negative about a diverticular vessel while retaining positive morphology.

The second inference is that the previous reassuring examination does not settle a newly symptomatic focal abnormality.

CT colonography is a credible modality competitor but cannot provide tissue sampling; repeating conventional CT is less useful after the already documented persistent lesion. The choices remain distinguishable without assuming a new numerical interval rule.

The recent examination and current course are explicit. The next node provides its own colonoscopy findings and mechanical symptoms; this explanation does not disclose resection. High-yield alarm-feature assessment.
suggestions: No required repair. In feedback, consider briefly explaining the tissue-sampling advantage over CT colonography so the closest alternative teaches a reusable distinction.
The sentence about prior procedural tolerance adds little to the new alarm-feature decision and could be shortened in a future authorized version.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: CT showed an inflamed sigmoid segment with a tract to the bladder dome and intravesical gas. decisionNodes.currentUpdate: CT showed sigmoid wall thickening and adjacent fat stranding, with no collection, extraluminal gas or obstruction. By reassessment her pain was improving, pulse was 78/min and temperature 37.1 C. She drank and ate without vomiting, took no immunosuppressive medicine and managed her usual activities independently. She could return for reassessment. Her history included two antibiotic-associated C. difficile infections.

answerChoices.label: Use oral hydration and analgesia with early reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The CT and observed course support a selected nonantibiotic outpatient plan. Give explicit return instructions for worsening pain, fever or inability to maintain intake.

answerChoices.label: Use inpatient intravenous antibiotics with serial reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: Admission is appropriate when illness severity or oral-intake failure warrants it. Her current trajectory and oral tolerance support outpatient care.
